category: Subordinators of place, and relative connectors

entries.meaning: The informal American twin of anywhere, built on place instead of the -where stem. It is a real Americanism — British English does not have it — and it is unremarkable in conversation and in fiction dialogue, but it is a register choice and not a meaning choice, so edited prose puts anywhere back. Note the spelling: closed up for the pro-form, two words for the ordinary noun (any place you can name).
examples: Sit anyplace you want — nobody saved seats.
We couldn't find anyplace that was still open past nine.
Anyplace the road narrows to one lane, expect a wait.
He'd have followed that team anyplace they played.
You can't smoke anyplace there's a kid within fifty feet.
She'll eat anyplace they keep the pie under glass.
entries.русский: где угодно; куда угодно — разг., амер. вариант anywhere; редактор правит на anywhere
entries.register: informal, chiefly American — ordinary in speech and casual writing, changed to anywhere by copy editors
entries.type: subordinating; also a place adverb (we didn't go anyplace) and a pronoun (anyplace is fine)
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (free choice)
entries.pattern: [main clause] anyplace [that] [clause]. · Anyplace [that] [clause], [main clause]. · [negated main clause] anyplace [clause] — the negative-polarity use. · [main clause] anyplace [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded, as in anyplace the dog can't get to.
entries.punctuation: Exactly the anywhere rule: no comma when the clause follows the main clause, comma after it when the clause is fronted, and never a comma on either side of the optional that.
entries.variants: anywhere (the standard equivalent, available in every position anyplace occupies); any place as two words is the literal noun phrase, not this pro-form
entries.see also: anywhere, someplace, everyplace, no place, anywheres

entries.meaning: Marks every location as equally acceptable — the choice is open and no place is excluded. Against its neighbors: everywhere sweeps across all locations at once, wherever leaves open which single one turns out to apply, and anywhere says the pick simply does not matter.
examples: Sit anywhere you like — the seats aren't assigned.
You can't park anywhere the curb is painted red.
Anywhere the trail crosses water, expect mud for the next half mile.
She would have followed that band anywhere they toured.
We couldn't find a motel anywhere that wasn't already booked.
He'll take a job anywhere he can bike to.
He's happy anyplace there's a decent taco truck.
entries.русский: где угодно; куда угодно; при отрицании — нигде, никуда — придаточное места
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: subordinating; also a place adverb (I looked, but I couldn't find it anywhere) and a pronoun (anywhere is fine with me)
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (free choice)
entries.pattern: [main clause] anywhere [that] [clause]. · Anywhere [that] [clause], [main clause]. · [negated main clause] anywhere [clause] — the negative-polarity use, as in you can't park anywhere the curb is red. · [main clause] anywhere [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded, as in anywhere the dog can't get to.
entries.punctuation: No comma when the anywhere clause follows the main clause; comma after it when it is fronted. The optional that never takes a comma before or after it.
entries.variants: anyplace (informal, chiefly American)

entries.meaning: The -s is the old adverbial genitive that standard English froze in always, besides, nowadays, and unawares and then stopped adding; regional American speech kept adding it. So anywheres is a survival rather than a blunder — but it is firmly nonstandard now, and an American meets it in Twain, in dialogue by Faulkner and Caldwell, and in rural speech from northern New England through the Ozarks, essentially nowhere else in print.
examples: There wasn't anywheres we could tie up the raft before dark.
He never went anywheres his mother didn't know about.
You won't cut hay like that anywheres the ground stays this wet.
I don't reckon there's anywheres around here a body can get a hot meal.
She won't shop anywheres they don't take a check.
It ain't anywheres near as far as the map makes it look.
entries.русский: где угодно — диал., прост.: нестандартная форма anywhere с -s
entries.register: dialectal and nonstandard — regional American speech and the dialect writing that records it; never correct in edited prose
entries.type: subordinating; more often a plain place adverb
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (free choice); relative clause hosted by a place pro-form
entries.pattern: [negated main clause] anywheres [clause]. · [main clause] anywheres [that] [clause]. · [main clause] anywheres [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded. · not … anywheres near [noun] — the frame in which it is heard most often.
entries.punctuation: The anywhere rule unchanged: no comma when the clause trails, comma after a fronted clause, no comma around the optional that. The -s affects nothing but the register.
entries.variants: anywhere (the standard form); somewheres, nowheres, everywheres (the same -s on the rest of the set)

entries.meaning: The informal American counterpart of everywhere. It is the weakest member of its family: anyplace and someplace are unremarkable in educated American speech, while everyplace reads as distinctly more casual and more rural. Nothing about the meaning changes — this is register only.
examples: Everyplace we stopped, the same three songs were playing.
Kudzu came up everyplace the county had cleared brush.
She left a note everyplace he was bound to look.
The chain has a store everyplace there's an interstate exit.
Everyplace the roof had been patched, it leaked worse than before.
They'll ship everyplace the mail truck goes.
entries.русский: везде, где; повсюду — разг., амер. вариант everywhere
entries.register: informal, chiefly American; the least-used member of the -place set and the one an editor is quickest to change
entries.type: subordinating; also a place adverb (we looked everyplace)
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (universal)
entries.pattern: Everyplace [that] [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] everyplace [that] [clause]. · [main clause] everyplace [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded.
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted everyplace clause, none when it trails, and no comma on either side of the optional that — the everywhere rule exactly.
entries.variants: everywhere (the standard equivalent, always available); every place as two words is the ordinary noun phrase, not this pro-form
entries.see also: everywhere, anyplace, someplace, no place, everywheres

entries.meaning: Says the main clause holds true at every location without exception. Where anywhere offers a free pick from many places, everywhere covers all of them simultaneously, which is why it so often opens the sentence as a sweeping scene-setter.
examples: Everywhere I go, somebody asks about the accent.
Bluebonnets came up everywhere the county had reseeded.
Everywhere the fire had passed, the ground was still warm two days later.
She left sticky notes everywhere he was likely to look.
Everywhere that the map showed a paved road, we found a dirt track.
The company ships everywhere the postal service delivers to.
The same chain restaurant turns up everywhere the interstate has an exit.
entries.русский: везде, где; повсюду, где — придаточное места со значением «во всех местах»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: subordinating; also a place adverb (I looked everywhere)
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (universal)
entries.pattern: Everywhere [that] [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] everywhere [that] [clause]. · [main clause] everywhere [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded, as in everywhere the light gets to.
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted everywhere clause; none when it follows the main clause. The optional that never takes a comma on either side.
entries.variants: everyplace (informal, chiefly American)

entries.meaning: Carries the same old adverbial -s as anywheres and nowheres — the ending standard English kept in always and besides and stopped extending. Of the three, everywheres is the least often heard and the least often written down; dialect novelists reach for anywheres and nowheres far more freely. Treat it as a marker of a speaker's region and generation, never as a stylistic option.
examples: Everywheres we went that summer, somebody wanted to talk about the flood.
He'd been everywheres the railroad ran, and then some.
There was ice everywheres the sun hadn't reached by noon.
Everywheres that creek gets out of its banks, the fences go with it.
She'd looked everywheres she could think of and still come up empty.
They sell that syrup everywheres the trucks stop.
entries.русский: везде — диал., прост.: нестандартная форма everywhere с -s
entries.register: dialectal and nonstandard, and the rarest of the -s forms — regional American speech and the dialect fiction that records it
entries.type: subordinating; more often a plain place adverb
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (universal)
entries.pattern: Everywheres [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] everywheres [clause]. · [main clause] everywheres [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded.
entries.punctuation: The everywhere rule: comma after a fronted clause, none when it trails. The -s changes nothing about the pointing.
entries.variants: everywhere (the standard form); anywheres, somewheres, nowheres (the same -s on the rest of the set)

entries.meaning: The informal American negative of the -place set, matching anyplace, someplace, and everyplace. It substitutes for nowhere in the ordinary post-verbal slot and nowhere else: the emphatic fronted construction, the noun (the middle of nowhere), and the fixed idioms all belong to nowhere alone.
examples: There was no place we could park within six blocks of the ballpark.
By ten o'clock there was no place in town still serving food.
The dog had no place to run that wasn't fenced.
He had no place he could go once the shift ended.
We looked for an hour and found no place the kids could swim.
Off that exit there's no place I'd want to spend the night.
entries.русский: негде, некуда; нет места, где — разг., амер. вариант nowhere; вперёд не выносится
entries.register: informal, chiefly American
entries.type: subordinating (negative); also a place adverb and a noun phrase (forty miles of no place)
entries.clause type: relative clause hosted by a negative place pro-form
entries.pattern: [there is/was] no place [that] [clause]. · [subject] [verb] no place [that] [clause]. · [main clause] no place [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded, as in no place I'd want to eat at.
entries.punctuation: No comma before the clause — it always narrows, so it is restrictive. And note the one syntactic difference from nowhere: no place does not front for inversion. Nowhere does the lease say you can sublet is idiomatic; No place does the lease say is not. Write it as two words — the one-word noplace is a further informal step that most American editors reject.
entries.variants: nowhere (the standard equivalent, and the only one of the two that can be fronted); noplace (one word, more informal still)

entries.meaning: The negative member of the somewhere / anywhere / everywhere set: it denies that any location satisfies the clause. Note that the clause after it is a relative clause with the relative word usually dropped, not a true adverbial clause — which is why that can be inserted (nowhere that still served food) but a comma cannot.
examples: There was nowhere we could park within six blocks of the stadium.
By ten o'clock there was nowhere that still served hot food.
Nowhere does the lease say you can sublet.
The kid had nowhere he could go after school, so the library became it.
Nowhere is the difference clearer than in the third-quarter numbers.
Off that exit there's nowhere I'd want to eat at.
We drove around for an hour and found no place the dog could run off leash.
entries.русский: нигде, никуда; негде, некуда — отрицательное место; при выносе вперёд требует инверсии
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: subordinating (negative); also a place adverb and a noun (the middle of nowhere)
entries.clause type: relative clause hosted by a negative place pro-form; with fronting, a negative adverbial
entries.pattern: [there is/was] nowhere [that] [clause]. · [subject] [verb] nowhere [that] [clause]. · Nowhere [auxiliary or be] [subject] [rest of clause] — fronted, with subject–auxiliary inversion. · [main clause] nowhere [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded, as in nowhere I'd want to eat at.
entries.punctuation: No comma before the clause that follows nowhere — it always narrows, so it is restrictive. Fronted nowhere takes no comma either, but it forces inversion: Nowhere does the lease say…, never Nowhere the lease says….
entries.variants: no place (informal, chiefly American)

entries.meaning: Standard nowhere with the old adverbial genitive -s that survives in always and besides. It belongs to the same regional grammar as ain't and the double negative, and it reaches print almost only as recorded speech: Huck Finn uses it constantly, and it is still live in rural speech from northern New England through the Ozarks. It is never a formal option — outside dialogue it is an error, not a choice.
examples: There warn't nowheres we could tie up till after dark.
He had nowheres to sleep and no money for a room.
There's nowheres around here a man can get his boots fixed anymore.
She wouldn't go nowheres her sister hadn't been first.
That's nowheres near enough lumber to finish the porch.
They hunted all afternoon and got nowheres the sheriff hadn't already looked.
entries.русский: нигде — диал., прост.: форма nowhere с -s, обычна в двойном отрицании
entries.register: dialectal and nonstandard — regional American speech and the dialect fiction that records it, Mark Twain's above all
entries.type: subordinating (negative); more often a plain place adverb
entries.clause type: relative clause hosted by a negative place pro-form
entries.pattern: [there is/was] nowheres [clause]. · [subject] [verb] nowheres [that] [clause]. · not … nowheres — the double negative, which is ordinary grammar in the dialects that have this word. · nowheres near [noun] — the frame that has spread furthest beyond the dialect.
entries.punctuation: No comma before the clause. Note that nowheres, unlike standard nowhere, does not front with subject–auxiliary inversion: the dialects that use it build emphasis with a doubled negative (there warn't nowheres to go), not with Nowheres did….
entries.variants: nowhere (the standard form); no place (informal but with standard syntax); anywheres, somewheres, everywheres

entries.meaning: The informal American twin of somewhere, and the most natural-sounding of the -place set — plenty of careful American speakers use it without noticing. It carries the spacing distinction that the -where forms never have to make: someplace quiet is the pro-form, some place I've never heard of is an ordinary noun plus a relative clause, and only the closed-up spelling belongs to this entry.
examples: We need someplace the whole crew can sit down at once.
He's looking for someplace he can leave the boat over the winter.
Let's eat someplace that doesn't have a drive-through.
She stashed the deed someplace even the lawyer couldn't find.
Someplace the kids can burn off an afternoon, that's what this town lacks.
Get off at the next exit and stop someplace they sell coffee.
entries.русский: где-нибудь, куда-нибудь — разг., амер. вариант somewhere
entries.register: informal, chiefly American — common in educated American speech and in fiction dialogue, replaced by somewhere in formal prose
entries.type: subordinating; also a place adverb (I left it someplace) and a pronoun
entries.clause type: relative clause hosted by an indefinite place pro-form
entries.pattern: [main clause] someplace [that] [clause]. · [main clause] someplace [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded. · Someplace [that] [clause], [main clause] — the whole phrase fronted as a topic and resumed by that's or there.
entries.punctuation: No comma before the clause — it says what sort of place is wanted, so it is restrictive. A comma appears only when the whole someplace phrase is fronted as a topic and the main clause picks it up again.
entries.variants: somewhere (the standard equivalent); some place as two words is the literal noun phrase, not this pro-form

entries.meaning: Names an unspecified location and then describes it with a clause. Strictly this is a relative construction rather than a place conjunction — somewhere is the head and the clause modifies it — but learners meet it in exactly the same slot as anywhere and everywhere, and it takes the same optional that.
examples: I need somewhere I can spread out all these papers.
They want somewhere the kids can run around without getting yelled at.
Let's find someplace that isn't a chain restaurant.
He keeps a spare key somewhere only his sister knows about.
She's looking for somewhere she can practice without the neighbors calling the police.
Somewhere the kids can run off some energy, that's what this trip is missing.
Park someplace the tow trucks won't bother checking.
entries.русский: где-нибудь, куда-нибудь; там, где — неопределённое место с придаточным
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: subordinating; also a place adverb (I left it somewhere) and a pronoun (somewhere in Ohio is far enough)
entries.clause type: relative clause hosted by an indefinite place pro-form
entries.pattern: [main clause] somewhere [that] [clause]. · [main clause] somewhere [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded, as in somewhere only his sister knows about. · Somewhere [that] [clause], [main clause] — the whole phrase fronted as a topic and picked up again by that's or there.
entries.punctuation: No comma before the clause — it identifies which sort of place is wanted, so it is restrictive. A comma appears only when the whole somewhere phrase is fronted as a topic and the main clause resumes it.
entries.variants: someplace (informal, chiefly American)

entries.meaning: Means "from what place" or "from which place." The from is already baked into the word, which makes from whence strictly redundant — but it is in the King James Bible and in Shakespeare, so it has four centuries of cover. Set against its partners: whence is the source, whither the destination, where the location.
examples: Return the stone whence it came.
He never said whence the money had come.
Investigators traced the outbreak to a single farm, whence the shipments had gone out to nine states.
"I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help."
The company moved its charter back to Delaware, whence it had come twenty years earlier.
The village whence his family came no longer appears on any map.
Nobody could establish whence the rumor had started.
entries.русский: откуда — устар., книжн.: место-источник
entries.register: archaic, literary
entries.type: subordinating; also a relative adverb
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (source); relative clause of origin; noun clause (indirect question)
entries.pattern: [main clause] whence [clause]. · [place noun], whence [clause]. · [place noun] whence [clause] — restrictive, no comma. · [verb of knowing/asking] whence [subject] [verb] — embedded, statement word order. · [main clause] from whence [clause] — the long-established redundant form.
entries.punctuation: Comma before whence when the clause merely adds information about a place already named; no comma when the clause completes the main clause or answers an implied question.
entries.variants: from whence (redundant but long established); whencesoever (archaic)

entries.meaning: The -soever intensification of whence, meaning "from absolutely any place that." Its whole purpose is the same as wheresoever's: to close loopholes by sounding exhaustive, which is why revenue and estate drafters kept it long after the word died in prose. Set against its partners, whencesoever is the source, whithersoever the destination, wheresoever the location.
examples: The duty is charged on goods whencesoever imported into the territory.
The trustee shall gather in the income of the estate, whencesoever arising.
Whencesoever the report had come, it was on the governor's desk by noon.
He would take help whencesoever it was offered, and ask no questions after.
The parish was bound to relieve any traveler in want, whencesoever he came.
Rumor, whencesoever it begins, is not easily called back.
entries.русский: откуда бы ни — устар., юр.: из любого источника, откуда бы ни поступило
entries.register: archaic; survives in scriptural cadence and in old customs and revenue drafting
entries.type: subordinating; also a relative adverb
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (source, universal); relative clause of origin
entries.pattern: [main clause] whencesoever [clause]. · Whencesoever [clause], [main clause]. · [noun] whencesoever [past participle] — the reduced statutory formula, as in goods whencesoever imported. · [noun] whencesoever [present participle] — as in income whencesoever arising.
entries.punctuation: The wheresoever rule: comma after a fronted clause, none when it trails. The reduced participial formula takes no comma at all — income whencesoever arising is one noun phrase.
entries.variants: whence (the plain form); whencesoe'er (poetic); from whatever source, from wherever (the living paraphrases)

entries.meaning: The workhorse of the category, and the one word that belongs to both families in this file. As an adverbial subordinator it locates the whole event (put it where I can see it). As a relative adverb it modifies a place noun and can be swapped for in which (the room where we met = the room in which we met). It also drifts into abstract territory, meaning "in cases in which" (where the law is silent, custom governs), which is standard in legal and academic prose.
examples: Put the boxes back where you found them.
Where the sidewalk ends, the gravel road starts.
This is the diner where we had breakfast every Sunday for six years.
We spent August in Bar Harbor, where my grandmother still keeps a house.
Nobody could tell me where the registration desk was.
Where the contract is silent, state law fills the gap.
He'll argue where most people would just walk away.
entries.pronunciation note: unstressed as a conjunction but not reduced; it never falls together with were /wər/
entries.русский: где; куда; там, где — место; также относительное «в котором» и косвенный вопрос «где»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: subordinating; also a relative adverb and an interrogative
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place; relative clause modifying a place noun; noun clause (indirect question)
entries.pattern: [main clause] where [clause]. · Where [clause], [main clause]. · [place noun] where [clause]. · [place noun], where [clause], [rest of sentence]. · [verb of knowing/asking] where [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when the place clause follows the main clause. Comma after a fronted where clause. As a relative adverb the general rule applies: no commas if the clause narrows which place is meant (the town where I was born), commas on both sides if the place is already identified (Tulsa, where I was born, has changed). Never a comma before an indirect question (ask where it is, not ask, where it is).
entries.variants: none in standard American English; at which / in which is the formal relative equivalent
entries.see also: wherever, wherein, when, which, whence, whither

entries.meaning: The all here is not the ordinary quantifier but an exhaustiveness marker welded to the wh- word: Where did you go? invites one answer, Where all did you go? asks for the whole itinerary. Standard English has no single word for the distinction and has to paraphrase, which is why the construction is so stable in the regions that have it — and why it is worth recognizing rather than correcting when you meet it.
examples: Where all did you go on that trip?
I don't know where all she's lived since college.
Where all have they put these stores now?
He couldn't remember where all he'd left his tools.
Ask her where all the family is coming in from.
Where all did y'all look before you called me?
entries.русский: где именно, во всех каких местах — диал. (юг США): вопрос требует перечислить все места
entries.register: dialectal — Southern and South Midland American; unremarkable in speech across that region and absent from edited prose everywhere
entries.type: subordinating (interrogative); also an interrogative adverb in direct questions
entries.clause type: noun clause (indirect question, exhaustive)
entries.pattern: Where all [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? — direct question, with inversion. · [verb of asking/knowing] where all [subject] [verb] — embedded, statement word order. · Where all [subject] [verb] [preposition]? — stranded. · Where [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] all? — the all floated to the end of the clause.
entries.punctuation: No comma between where and all, and none before the embedded clause. The direct question takes a question mark; the embedded clause takes none.
entries.variants: who all, what all (the same all on the other wh- words); all the places (that) (the standard paraphrase)
entries.see also: where, who all, what all, whereabouts

entries.respell: the at is unstressed and normally reduced to /ət/
entries.meaning: Where already means "at what place," so the trailing at is redundant, and that redundancy is the whole basis of the schoolroom joke ("Where are you at?" "Between the A and the T"). It is nonetheless one of the most common features of casual American speech, cutting across region, race, and class — treat it as informal rather than illiterate, but keep it out of writing. One offshoot escaped the stigma completely: the frozen idiom where it's at, meaning "the thing that actually matters," is standard colloquial English and no editor blinks at it.
examples: Do you know where the extra chairs are at?
"Where you at?" is the entire text message in this family.
Nobody could tell me where the trailhead was at.
He asked where I was at on the quarterly report.
She never says where she's at, only when she'll be back.
Comfortable shoes and a ten-minute commute — that's where it's at.
entries.русский: где — прост.: избыточное at в конце придаточного, в русском не отражается
entries.register: nonstandard; extremely widespread in casual American speech in every region, and one of the most heavily corrected features in American schools
entries.type: subordinating — plain where with a pleonastic stranded at
entries.clause type: noun clause (indirect question of place); adverbial clause of place
entries.pattern: [verb of asking/knowing] where [subject] [verb] at. · Where [auxiliary] [subject] at? — the direct question. · [main clause] where [subject] [verb] at. · where it's at — the frozen idiom, which is a different animal.
entries.punctuation: No comma anywhere in it; it points exactly like plain where. Note that the at attaches to the end of its own clause, not to where — which is why the headword is where … at and not a single word, and why it can be separated from where by an entire clause (where you said the key was at).
entries.variants: plain where (the standard form — the at contributes nothing); whereat as one word is an unrelated archaic relative meaning "at which," documented in 12-formal-archaic

entries.meaning: Asks for a rough location where where asks for an exact one — "in what general area." Americans use the direct question freely (Whereabouts are you from?) but rarely embed it as a conjunction; She asked whereabouts I lived reads as British. The homograph noun, his whereabouts, is fully standard American and takes either a singular or a plural verb.
examples: Whereabouts in Ohio did you grow up?
She asked whereabouts I'd left the car.
I couldn't tell the ranger whereabouts on the trail we'd seen the bear.
Whereabouts are you staying — downtown or out by the airport?
Nobody is quite sure whereabouts the property line actually runs.
entries.русский: где примерно, в каком районе — разг.: спрашивает о приблизительном месте
entries.register: informal; the embedded use is chiefly British and Irish rather than American
entries.type: subordinating (interrogative); also an interrogative adverb and a plural noun (his whereabouts are unknown)
entries.clause type: noun clause (indirect question of approximate place)
entries.pattern: Whereabouts [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? — direct question, with inversion. · Whereabouts [prepositional phrase] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? — as in Whereabouts in Ohio did you grow up? · [verb of asking/knowing] whereabouts [subject] [verb] — embedded, statement word order. · [verb of asking/knowing] whereabouts [prepositional phrase] [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: No comma before it in either use. The direct question takes a question mark; the embedded clause takes none.
entries.variants: whereabout (rare singular); the identical noun whereabouts (his whereabouts are unknown)

entries.meaning: Built from where + as, and originally meaning "at which place" — which is why it sits in this file. Modern American English keeps two descendants of that original sense. The living one is contrast: X holds, and by contrast Y holds. Unlike coordinating but, whereas subordinates, so its clause can be moved to the front; unlike while, it carries no possible time reading. The fossil one is the legal preamble, where whereas means "given the fact that" and introduces the background recitals of a contract.
examples: Her brother took the corporate job, whereas she went into teaching.
Whereas the 2019 model had a physical dial, the new one is all touchscreen.
Federal law caps the fee at fifty dollars, whereas state law leaves it open.
WHEREAS, the Seller is the record owner of the property described in Exhibit A; and WHEREAS, the Buyer desires to purchase that property; NOW, THEREFORE, the parties agree as follows.
He remembers every phone number he has ever had, whereas I can't reliably recall my own zip code.
entries.русский: тогда как — противопоставление; в преамбуле договора (юр.) «принимая во внимание, что»
entries.register: formal; the preamble use is legal
entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of contrast; in legal drafting, a recital
entries.pattern: Whereas [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], whereas [clause]. · WHEREAS, [clause]; WHEREAS, [clause]; NOW, THEREFORE, [operative clause].
entries.punctuation: Always a comma before whereas when it follows the main clause — the contrast it draws is never restrictive. Comma after it when fronted. In contract recitals, successive whereas clauses are separated by semicolons, and the last one ends with ; NOW, THEREFORE,.
entries.variants: none; note that British whilst is not an American substitute for anything in this entry

entries.meaning: The emphatic form of wherever, built with the old intensifying suffix -soever that also gives whatsoever and whomsoever. It means "in absolutely any place that," and its whole modern function is to sound total and unloopholed, which is why estate and tax drafters keep it alive.
examples: The bearer shall have safe passage wheresoever he may travel within the realm.
Wheresoever the Company does business, these standards apply without exception.
He swore he would follow her wheresoever she went.
The duty is charged on the decedent's assets wheresoever situated.
Wheresoever two or three are gathered together, there is a committee meeting waiting to happen.
entries.русский: где бы ни; повсюду, где — устар., юр.: «где бы ни находилось»
entries.register: archaic; survives in legal and ceremonial writing
entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (universal, emphatic)
entries.pattern: Wheresoever [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] wheresoever [clause]. · [noun] wheresoever [past participle] — the legal formula, as in assets wheresoever situated.
entries.punctuation: The same rule as wherever: comma after a fronted clause, none when it trails. The reduced participial formula takes no comma at all.
entries.variants: wheresoe'er (poetic), whereso (archaic)

entries.meaning: Means "in any place that," "in every place that," or — the concessive reading — "it doesn't matter where." Where plain where points at one identifiable place, wherever leaves the place open or sweeps across all of them. It is the place member of the -ever fused-relative family along with whatever, whoever, and whenever.
examples: Wherever she goes, people recognize her.
Set the tripod down wherever the ground is level.
Wherever you end up living, keep the heavy coat.
The company will match the offer, wherever it comes from.
He falls asleep wherever he sits down for more than ten minutes.
Wherever the money went, it certainly didn't go into the roof.
entries.русский: где бы ни; куда бы ни; везде, где — обобщающее и уступительное место
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: subordinating; also a fused relative
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (universal); concessive clause of place
entries.pattern: Wherever [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] wherever [clause]. · [main clause], wherever [clause] — afterthought, with a comma. · Wherever it is [that] [clause] — the emphatic cleft. · Where ever [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? — two words, and only in an emphatic question.
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted wherever clause. No comma when it follows the main clause, unless it is tacked on as an afterthought (I'll find it, wherever it ended up).
entries.variants: where'er, whereso'er (poetic); no matter where (exact phrasal equivalent in the concessive sense)

entries.meaning: Means "to what place" or "to which place" — the destination counterpart of whence (source) and where (location). It is dead in American speech and alive in exactly two registers: the King James cadence (whither thou goest) and the op-ed headline (Whither the middle class?), where it means "where is this heading?"
examples: "Whither thou goest, I will go."
Nobody asked whither the money was being wired.
They boarded a ship bound for a colony whither very few had gone willingly.
Whither American manufacturing?
He wandered off, whither nobody could say.
The families were moved to a second camp, whither the aid trucks rarely made it.
entries.pronunciation note: a homophone of wither for most Americans
entries.русский: куда — устар., книжн.: место-назначение
entries.register: archaic, literary
entries.type: subordinating; also a relative adverb
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (destination); relative clause of destination; noun clause
entries.pattern: [main clause] whither [clause]. · [place noun] whither [clause] — restrictive, no comma. · [place noun], whither [clause] — nonrestrictive, comma. · [verb of knowing/asking] whither [subject] [verb] — embedded, statement word order. · Whither [noun phrase]? — the verbless headline formula.
entries.punctuation: Comma before it when the clause adds information about a place already named; none when the clause completes the main clause. The headline formula takes a question mark and no verb at all.
entries.variants: whithersoever (archaic, emphatic)

entries.meaning: The -soever intensification of whither, meaning "to absolutely any place that." It completes the emphatic set: whencesoever is the source, whithersoever the destination, wheresoever the location. Like the rest of that set it does not intensify so much as change costume — the register jumps from neutral to scriptural, and nothing about the meaning is stronger than plain wherever. ---
examples: And I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest.
Whithersoever the ark was carried, the people followed after it.
The knight swore to attend his lord whithersoever he might ride.
He resolved to go whithersoever the work took him, and it took him to Ohio.
Whithersoever the current bore them, they had no oars to argue with it.
The commissioners may direct the relief fund whithersoever the need is greatest.
entries.русский: куда бы ни — устар., библ.: в любое место назначения
entries.register: archaic; scriptural and ceremonial — an American meets it in the King James Bible, in hymn text, and in period pastiche, and nowhere else
entries.type: subordinating; also a relative adverb
entries.clause type: adverbial clause of place (destination, universal); relative clause of destination
entries.pattern: Whithersoever [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] whithersoever [clause]. · [place noun] whithersoever [clause] — restrictive, no comma. · [noun] whithersoever [past participle] — the reduced formula, as in goods whithersoever consigned.
entries.punctuation: The wheresoever rule: comma after a fronted clause, none when it trails. The reduced participial formula takes no comma.
entries.variants: whither (the plain form); whithersoe'er (poetic); wherever, no matter where (the living equivalents)

entries.meaning: Means "by means of which" and attaches a clause to an abstract noun that names a mechanism. Despite the spelling it never means "where" — the town whereby I live is not English. It also has a narrow antecedent range: if the noun in front of it is not a method, procedure, or arrangement, whereby is the wrong word.
examples: They set up a system whereby every request gets a tracking number.
The union negotiated an arrangement whereby senior staff pick their shifts first.
There's a provision whereby the filing fee is waived for first-time applicants.
He described a process whereby the plastic is broken back down into its original monomers.
The bylaws create a mechanism whereby any two board members can call a special meeting.
The tenants stayed on under an arrangement whereby the landlord covered heat through March.
entries.русский: посредством которого; согласно которому — «by which» при существительном способа
entries.register: formal
entries.type: relative adverb
entries.clause type: restrictive relative clause modifying a noun of method (system, arrangement, process, rule, mechanism)
entries.pattern: [noun of method] whereby [subject] [verb]. · [preposition] [noun of method] whereby [clause] — as in under a system whereby claims are audited quarterly. · [verb] [determiner] [noun of method] whereby [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before whereby — the clause defines the arrangement it follows, so it is restrictive by nature. A nonrestrictive whereby is possible but so rare it reads as an error; use by which with commas instead. Whereby never begins a sentence, and it never takes a semicolon.
entries.variants: by which (the plain equivalent, always available)

entries.meaning: Means "for which reason" or, in its interrogative use, simply "why." Juliet's Wherefore art thou Romeo? asks why he has to be a Romeo, not where he is — the most consistently misread line in English. Modern American English keeps it in two places: the prayer for relief at the end of a legal pleading, and the frozen phrase the whys and wherefores. It is the one where- compound in this section that is not a subordinator, which is exactly why it takes a semicolon where whereupon takes a comma.
examples: "Wherefore art thou Romeo?"
The defendant failed to appear; wherefore the court entered judgment by default.
She wanted to know all the whys and wherefores before she signed anything.
WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter judgment in her favor and award costs.
The notice went to the wrong address. Wherefore, the thirty-day clock never started running.
Wherefore should any of us care what that committee thinks?
entries.русский: вследствие чего, посему; устар. «почему» — юр.; в whys and wherefores — «причины»
entries.register: archaic; survives in legal drafting and one fixed noun phrase
entries.type: conjunctive adverb ("for which reason"); also an archaic interrogative adverb and, in the fixed plural, a noun
entries.clause type: independent clause of result or consequence; interrogative clause of reason
entries.pattern: [independent clause]; wherefore [independent clause]. · [independent clause]. Wherefore, [independent clause]. · WHEREFORE, [subject] [verb] — the prayer for relief that closes a legal pleading. · Wherefore [auxiliary or verb] [subject] …? — the archaic interrogative meaning "why." · the whys and wherefores — fixed noun phrase.
entries.punctuation: Wherefore connects two independent clauses the way therefore does, so it needs a semicolon or a period before it — he defaulted, wherefore the lease terminated is a comma splice, and he defaulted; wherefore the lease terminated is the repair. Do not confuse it with whereupon, which is a subordinator and takes a comma. When wherefore opens its own sentence it takes a comma after it (WHEREFORE, Plaintiff prays…). The interrogative use inverts the subject and ends in a question mark.
entries.variants: whys and wherefores (fixed plural noun); therefore, hence, thus (the living equivalents, all punctuated the same way)

entries.meaning: Means "from which." It is the least successful of the where- compounds, and the reason is easy to see: English already owned whence, which says the same thing in one syllable and had four centuries of scriptural backing. Wherefrom was left as the drafter's word — you find it in title chains and probate files, where the whole point is to name a source without ambiguity — and even there it now looks like a slip of the pen to most readers.
examples: The corporation shall disclose the account wherefrom the payment was drawn.
He would never name the source wherefrom the letters came.
The spring wherefrom the whole town drew its water went dry in August.
The deed recites the earlier grant wherefrom the plaintiff's title derives.
She returned at last to the same small parish wherefrom she had been sent out.
The record nowhere shows the fund wherefrom the disbursement was made.
entries.русский: откуда, из которого — устар.: «from which», редчайшее в семье where-
entries.register: archaic, and the rarest of the whole where- family — old deeds, old wills, and period prose
entries.type: relative adverb
entries.clause type: relative clause of source, restrictive or nonrestrictive
entries.pattern: [noun] wherefrom [clause] — restrictive, no comma. · [noun], wherefrom [clause], [rest of sentence] — nonrestrictive. · [noun of origin] wherefrom [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: No comma when the clause defines the noun in front of it; a comma when the noun is already identified and the clause merely adds. Like every where- relative except wherefore, it cannot begin a sentence and never takes a semicolon.
entries.variants: from which (the plain equivalent, and the one a modern reader expects); whence (the older single word for the same idea); whereof, whereat, whereon, wherewith (the same family)
entries.see also: whence, whereof, whereunto, wherein, in which

entries.meaning: Means "in which," covering both literal containment (a country wherein no one pays for medicine) and the abstract sense "in which respect" (wherein it differs from the standard form). Its everyday substitutes are in which and, for physical places, plain where.
examples: He described a country wherein no one pays out of pocket for medicine.
The statute has a clause wherein "business day" is defined as excluding federal holidays.
Both candidates promised reform — wherein lies the problem, since neither would define it.
She published a memoir wherein she named half the department by name.
The contract is silent as to remedies, wherein it differs sharply from the standard form.
entries.русский: в котором; в чём — книжн.: «in which»
entries.register: formal, literary
entries.type: relative adverb
entries.clause type: relative clause of location or of respect — restrictive or nonrestrictive
entries.pattern: [noun] wherein [clause]. · [noun], wherein [clause], [rest of sentence]. · wherein lies [noun phrase] — fixed inversion.
entries.punctuation: No comma when the clause narrows the noun (a clause wherein the deadline is defined); comma before it when the noun is already fully identified. The fixed wherein lies the problem is normally preceded by a comma or a dash.
entries.variants: in which (the plain equivalent); therein is the demonstrative counterpart, not a connector

entries.meaning: Means "of which" or "of what." In modern American English it survives in essentially one place: the closing attestation line of a contract. Everywhere else, of which has replaced it entirely, and the value whereof now reads as deliberate legalese.
examples: IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have executed this Agreement as of the date first written above.
"Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent."
He spoke at length of matters whereof he had no direct knowledge.
She produced a receipt, the authenticity whereof was immediately disputed.
The estate, the value whereof exceeds two million dollars, passes into the trust.
entries.русский: о котором; которого — устар., юр.: «of which»; IN WITNESS WHEREOF — «в удостоверение чего»
entries.register: archaic; survives in one legal formula
entries.type: relative adverb
entries.clause type: relative clause meaning "of which" or "of what"
entries.pattern: [noun] whereof [clause]. · [noun], the [attribute] whereof [verb phrase]. · IN WITNESS WHEREOF, [clause].
entries.punctuation: In the witness formula, a comma follows the whole phrase (IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have executed…). Elsewhere, no comma when the clause defines the noun before it; a comma when it merely adds.
entries.variants: the same pattern once produced whereto ("to which"), wherewith ("with which"), whereat ("at which"), and whereon ("on which") — all now archaic

entries.meaning: Means "to which." It is the -unto member of the family, and its ordinary habitat is the Authorized Version and the prose written in imitation of it — a purpose, an office, or a calling that something is directed toward. Modern English says to which, and in the one place the -unto shape is still alive it is not this word but its demonstrative cousin: the parties have hereunto set their hands closes contracts that were signed this morning.
examples: He proved faithful in the office whereunto he had been called.
The instrument creates an easement whereunto the adjoining owner is entitled in perpetuity.
She had no notion of the end whereunto all this labor was tending.
The witness could not name the fund whereunto the money had been transferred.
There is a purpose whereunto every one of these trials is bent.
The charter recites the uses whereunto the endowment shall be applied.
entries.русский: к которому; для чего — устар., библ.: «to which»
entries.register: archaic; scriptural, and a fossil in older legal drafting
entries.type: relative adverb
entries.clause type: relative clause of destination or purpose, restrictive or nonrestrictive
entries.pattern: [noun] whereunto [clause] — restrictive, no comma. · [noun], whereunto [clause], [rest of sentence] — nonrestrictive. · [noun of office or purpose] whereunto [subject] [verb] — as in the office whereunto he was called.
entries.punctuation: No comma when the clause defines the noun before it; a comma when it merely adds. It cannot begin a sentence and never takes a semicolon. Do not confuse it with the demonstrative hereunto, which is not a connector at all and which sits in a signature block (have hereunto set their hands) with no clause after it.
entries.variants: whereto (the shorter form, equally archaic); to which (the plain modern equivalent); hereunto, thereunto (the demonstrative counterparts, still typed into American signature blocks every working day)
entries.see also: whereof, wherefrom, wherein, whither, in which

entries.meaning: Means "and immediately after that," chaining an event to the reaction it triggered. Compared with then, which is an adverb and therefore needs its own and or a semicolon, whereupon does the joining itself. Compared with whereby (method), whereupon is pure sequence. ---
examples: The fire alarm went off at 3 a.m., whereupon two hundred guests filed into the parking lot in bathrobes.
He asked for a raise, whereupon his manager changed the subject to parking.
The bill cleared the Senate, whereupon the House refused to take it up at all.
She set the pie on the windowsill, whereupon the dog took an immediate professional interest.
The pitcher argued the call, whereupon the umpire ejected him.
entries.русский: после чего; вслед за чем — присоединяет следствие ко всему предыдущему высказыванию
entries.register: formal
entries.type: relative adverb (continuative)
entries.clause type: nonrestrictive relative clause whose antecedent is the entire preceding clause
entries.pattern: [independent clause], whereupon [subject] [verb]. · [independent clause], whereupon [clause], [continuation]. · [noun of occasion] whereupon [clause] — rare and formal, as in the moment whereupon everything turned.
entries.punctuation: In the ordinary use — where the antecedent is the whole preceding clause — always a comma before it, never a semicolon and never nothing. This is the one that trips people up: whereupon looks like therefore and consequently, but it is a subordinator, not a conjunctive adverb, so it takes a comma where those take a semicolon. Its own neighbor wherefore goes the other way — semicolon — so the two cannot be punctuated alike. The rare use with a noun antecedent (the moment whereupon everything turned) is an ordinary restrictive relative and takes no comma at all. Whereupon also cannot begin a sentence, and the clause after it cannot stand alone.
entries.variants: upon which, at which point (both less formal, same meaning)

entries.meaning: As is a relative pronoun in only three environments: after such, after the same, and in a sentential relative like as I mentioned, where its antecedent is a whole clause. Everywhere else it is a subordinating conjunction of time, cause, or manner — a different word entirely. Regional American speech extends relative as to ordinary nouns (the man as sold me the truck), which is nonstandard and marked.
examples: He isn't the same person as he was ten years ago.
Bring only such tools as you'll actually need on the roof.
The dough will take as much flour as the humidity demands.
The flight was delayed, as everyone at the gate had predicted.
As the minutes show, the motion failed on a tie vote.
She got the same grade as I did, which still annoys me.
The budget, as you'll see on page four, was blown by March.
entries.русский: который — относительное только после such, the same, as much/many; либо «как» обо всей фразе
entries.register: neutral in the fixed frames; formal in the sentential use; nonstandard in the bare relative use
entries.type: relative pronoun (only after such, same, and as many/much); elsewhere a subordinating conjunction of time, cause, manner, or concession, a preposition (as a rule, hired as a temp), an adverb of degree (as tall), and half of the correlative as … as
entries.clause type: restrictive relative clause; sentential relative clause
entries.pattern: such [noun] as [clause]. · the same [noun] as [clause]. · as many/much [noun] as [clause]. · [main clause], as [clause] — sentential, trailing. · As [clause], [main clause] — sentential, fronted. · [subject], as [clause], [predicate] — sentential, interrupting.
entries.punctuation: No comma anywhere in the such / same / as…as frames. A sentential as clause is parenthetical: comma before it when it closes the sentence, comma after it when it opens, commas on both sides when it interrupts.
entries.variants: such as, the same as (the fixed frames)

entries.meaning: A relative pronoun that swallows a negative: there is no rule but has an exception means "no rule that does not have an exception." Because the negative is already inside it, the word needs a negative or a question above it to be licensed at all — strip the no and the sentence collapses, since there is a rule but has an exception is not English. That dependence is what makes it a genuinely different word from the but of slow but steady. Americans meet it in proverbs, in the King James Bible, and in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century prose; nobody produces it fresh.
examples: There is no rule but has its exception.
There is not a man among them but would swear to it in open court.
Who is there but has wished, at least once, to begin the whole thing over?
Not a day passed but she thought of that letter.
There breathes no sailor on this coast but knows that light.
Scarcely a family in the county but has lost somebody to the mill.
entries.русский: который не — устар.: относительное со встроенным отрицанием, требует отрицания в главном
entries.register: archaic and literary; alive in a handful of proverbs and otherwise a period form
entries.type: relative pronoun (negative) — a relative with its own negative built in; elsewhere a coordinating conjunction, a preposition (everyone but me), and a focusing adverb (but a child)
entries.clause type: restrictive relative clause, licensed only by a negative, an interrogative, or only in the clause above it
entries.pattern: [negated existential] but [verb phrase] — as in there is no one but knows it. · no / not a / scarcely a [noun] but [verb phrase]. · Who is there but [verb phrase]? — the rhetorical question. · never so [adjective] but [clause] — the concessive cousin, treated at but that.
entries.punctuation: No comma before it — the clause narrows the negated noun, so it is restrictive by nature. It cannot be fronted, cannot open a sentence, and never takes a semicolon. A comma there turns it into coordinating but and changes the sentence entirely: there is no rule, but it has exceptions says something different from there is no rule but has exceptions.
entries.variants: that … not, who … not, which … not (the modern paraphrases); but that, but what (the same negative but with an extra complementizer); but for (the conditional preposition, unrelated to this entry)
entries.see also: that, which, who, zero relative, but, but that

entries.meaning: The transparent, unpacked ancestor of wherefore — every where- compound is exactly "preposition + which," and this is what that one looks like spelled out. It has outlived the compound in the places where a writer needs to hang a consequence on a whole clause without starting a new sentence: opinions, recitals, and careful academic prose. Against which is why, which does the same job in ordinary English, for which reason is heavier by design.
examples: The notice was mailed to an address the company had abandoned two years earlier, for which reason the thirty-day period never began to run.
Two of the three appraisals were prepared by the seller's own broker, for which reason the court gave them little weight.
He had signed the waiver before reading a word of it, for which reason his objection came far too late.
The samples were stored well above the specified temperature, for which reason the results are reported here only as provisional.
The statute contains no severability clause, for which reason the whole section falls with the invalid subsection.
The witness had been in the room the entire time, for which reason her account was preferred to his.
entries.русский: по каковой причине; вследствие чего — книжн., юр.: развёрнутый эквивалент wherefore
entries.register: formal; judicial opinions, contract recitals, and old-fashioned expository prose
entries.type: relative connective — pied-piped preposition + relative determiner + noun; functionally a continuative relative
entries.clause type: nonrestrictive relative clause whose antecedent is the whole preceding clause
entries.pattern: [independent clause], for which reason [clause]. · [noun of cause], for which reason [clause]. · For which reason, [clause] — a fresh sentence, which only legal drafting does. · for which purpose / for which cause — the same frame with the noun changed.
entries.punctuation: A comma before it — it opens a nonrestrictive relative clause that cannot stand on its own. This is the trap: it means the same thing as therefore, so writers reach for the therefore pointing and produce the wrong mark. Therefore is a conjunctive adverb and needs a semicolon or a period; for which reason is a relative and takes a comma, exactly like whereupon. When legal drafting does start a sentence with it, a comma follows it as well (For which reason, the motion is denied.).
entries.variants: wherefore (the one-word archaic equivalent, and punctuated the opposite way); for which purpose, for which cause, on which account; therefore, hence, which is why (the living substitutes)
entries.see also: wherefore, which, whereupon, why, in which

entries.meaning: Before whoever took the job over, English said he that: a bare pronoun head with a relative clause hung on it, the whole thing meaning "any person who." Three habitats keep it alive — scripture and hymn (he that hath ears), proverb (he that goes a-borrowing goes a-sorrowing), and the maxims of equity (he that seeks equity must do equity). It has no gender-neutral form, which is one reason modern prose moved on to whoever and anyone who.
examples: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her."
He that goes a-borrowing goes a-sorrowing.
"They that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength."
He that comes into equity must come with clean hands.
Give the notice to him that holds the lease, not to the occupant.
They that sow the wind shall reap the whirlwind.
entries.русский: тот, кто — устар., библ.: предшественник whoever, без родовой нейтральности
entries.register: archaic; scripture, hymnody, proverb, and legal maxim — an American meets it in the King James Bible, in Shakespeare, in Franklin, and in the older sayings of the law
entries.type: fused-relative frame — a bare pronoun head plus relative that; equivalent to the modern one-word fused relative whoever
entries.clause type: restrictive relative clause with a pronoun head; the whole phrase functions as a noun phrase
entries.pattern: He that [verb phrase] + [main verb] — the phrase as subject. · He that [verb phrase], [imperative or resumptive clause] — the older pointing, licensed by a resumptive him or let him. · They that [verb phrase] + [main verb] — plural. · [verb/preposition] him that [verb phrase] — oblique case on the head. · He who [verb phrase] — the same frame with who, and the only version still written today.
entries.punctuation: Never a comma between the head pronoun and that — they are one phrase. The comma that period texts put after a long subject clause (He that hath ears to hear, let him hear) is licensed there by the resumptive let him; without a resumptive it is an error, so write He that hesitates is lost with no comma at all.
entries.variants: they that, she that, those that, him that, them that (the same frame inflected for number and case); he who, those who (the who version, still current); whoever, anyone who (the living equivalents); nonstandard them that survives in dialect (them that has, gets)
entries.see also: that, whoever, whosoever, who, the which

entries.meaning: Fronting the preposition along with which is the formal option; leaving it at the end of the clause is the normal spoken one. Both are correct American English — the old rule against ending a sentence with a preposition was never a rule of the language — so the choice is register, not grammar. What is real is the constraint the fronting creates: once a preposition stands in front, only which or whom can follow it, which means choosing the formal word order also forces the formal relative pronoun. Of which is worth a separate look, since it does double duty as the inanimate possessive (a house the roof of which leaks), where most writers now prefer whose.
examples: This is the cabinet in which the old contracts were stored.
The year in which the plant closed is still a sore subject in this town.
She described the conditions under which the samples had been held.
The account to which the wire was sent had been opened that same morning.
He kept a list of every town through which the line had once run.
There were four bidders, of which only two submitted complete packages.
The tools with which the repair was made were not the ones the manual specifies.
entries.русский: в котором — книжн.: предлог вынесен вперёд; в разговорной речи он уходит в конец
entries.register: formal; the stranded alternative (the box it came in) is the neutral spoken form and is equally correct
entries.type: relative pronoun with a pied-piped preposition
entries.clause type: relative clause — restrictive after a bare noun, nonrestrictive after a comma
entries.pattern: [noun] in which [subject] [verb] — restrictive. · [noun], in which [clause], [rest of sentence] — nonrestrictive. · [noun] [that / ∅] [subject] [verb] in — the stranded equivalent. · the identical frame with any preposition: of which, to which, for which, on which, with which, at which, by which, from which, under which, through which, upon which.
entries.punctuation: ✗ Never a comma between the preposition and which — the two move as one unit and belong to the same phrase. The clause itself follows the ordinary rule: no commas when it narrows which thing is meant (the cabinet in which the contracts were stored), commas on both sides when the thing is already identified (the north cabinet, in which the contracts were stored, was never locked). And note what the fronted preposition forbids: it ✗ blocks that and it blocks the zero relative, so the box in that it came and the box in it came are both impossible.
entries.variants: of which, to which, for which, on which, with which, at which, by which, from which, under which (the same construction with the preposition changed); the stranded that … in / ∅ … in (the ordinary spoken form); wherein, whereof, whereto, whereon, wherewith (the archaic one-word compounds for the same thing); of which doubles as the stiff possessive alternative to whose
entries.see also: which, whom, wherein, whereof, the manner in which, zero relative

entries.meaning: The default restrictive relative, usable for people, things, and animals alike. Against which: American editors keep that for clauses that narrow the reference and which for clauses that add — the comma and the word choice move together. Against who: both are correct for people restrictively, but who is preferred in formal writing. And note that the relative that is a different word from the complementizer that in I know that he left: the complementizer fills no gap and has no antecedent.
examples: The apartment that we looked at on Tuesday is already rented.
Anything that can go wrong on a Friday afternoon will.
She's the only person that still remembers how the old phone system worked.
This is the road that floods every single spring.
Nothing that the committee proposed made it into the final budget.
The one that got away was a twelve-pound striper.
This is the shelf that everything eventually gets dumped on.
entries.русский: который, что — относительное только в ограничительных придаточных, без запятой
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: relative pronoun; also a complementizer, a demonstrative determiner, and a degree adverb
entries.clause type: restrictive relative clause only; as a complementizer, a noun clause
entries.pattern: [noun] that [verb phrase] — subject relative, and that cannot be deleted. · [noun] that [subject] [verb] — object relative, and that may be deleted. · [noun] that [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded preposition, as in the chair that she sat on. · [noun] ∅ [subject] [verb] — the zero relative, object position only.
entries.punctuation: Never a comma before relative that. A comma marks a clause as nonrestrictive, and that cannot introduce a nonrestrictive clause; if the sentence wants a comma there, the word must be which (things) or who (people). That also cannot follow a preposition — the chair on that she sat is impossible; use on which or strand the preposition.
entries.variants: the zero relative ∅ in object position (the book I read)
entries.see also: which, who, what, whose, as, zero relative

entries.meaning: A fixed technical frame rather than a single connector: under which is the relative proper and the conditions is the head noun it modifies. It earns a place because it does something no single wh- word does — specify the conditions under which the warranty applies asks for the entire set of qualifying situations, where specify when the warranty applies asks only for an occasion. That is a real distinction, and it is why the phrase resists the editing that its bulk invites.
examples: The paper never states the conditions under which the samples were stored.
Section 4 sets out the conditions under which the deposit becomes nonrefundable.
The conditions under which the experiment was run bear no resemblance to a working kitchen.
We should settle in advance the conditions under which either side may walk away.
The manual is silent as to the conditions under which the alarm resets itself.
She wanted the conditions under which she would be released put in writing.
entries.русский: условия, при которых — книжн., научн.: предлог вынесен вперёд
entries.register: formal; scientific, technical, regulatory, and legal prose
entries.type: complex relative frame — head noun + pied-piped preposition + relative pronoun
entries.clause type: restrictive relative clause modifying conditions; the whole phrase serves as the subject or the object of the main clause
entries.pattern: the conditions under which [subject] [verb] + [main verb] — the phrase as subject. · [verb of specifying/describing] the conditions under which [clause] — as object. · [preposition] the conditions under which [clause]. · the circumstances under which / the terms under which / the rules under which — the same frame with the head noun changed.
entries.punctuation: No comma anywhere inside the frame, and — the one that gets missed — no comma between the frame and the main verb when the whole phrase is the subject: The conditions under which the test was run are not stated takes nothing before are, however long the clause has grown. The relative clause is restrictive, so it does not open with a comma either.
entries.variants: the circumstances under which, the terms under which, the conditions in which; the conditions whereunder (archaic legal); when or how (the lean substitutes an editor will suggest)
entries.see also: in which, the extent to which, the manner in which, which, where

entries.meaning: Names an amount and then defines it with a clause: the degree to which the model fits is "how well the model fits," packaged so it can sit in a subject slot. Against the extent to which, its nearest neighbor: degree leans toward intensity on a graded scale and extent toward reach or coverage, but in most sentences either will serve, and extent is the more common of the two in American academic writing.
examples: The degree to which the two accounts agree is itself the surprising part.
Nobody has measured the degree to which the subsidy actually changed behavior.
The finding depends entirely on the degree to which respondents understood the question.
The degree to which she had prepared for that hearing was obvious within five minutes.
The report says nothing about the degree to which the estimate is sensitive to the discount rate.
Reviewers disagreed about the degree to which the method was genuinely novel.
entries.русский: степень, в какой; насколько — книжн.: мера, поддающаяся оценке
entries.register: formal; academic, analytical, and evaluative prose
entries.type: complex relative frame — noun of measure + pied-piped preposition + relative pronoun
entries.clause type: restrictive relative clause modifying degree; the whole phrase behaves as a noun phrase, usually the subject or the object of a verb of measuring or judging
entries.pattern: The degree to which [subject] [verb] + [main verb] — the phrase as subject. · [verb of measuring/assessing] the degree to which [clause] — as object. · [preposition] the degree to which [clause] — as in depends on the degree to which.
entries.punctuation: No comma inside the frame, none before to which, and none between the whole phrase and the main verb when the phrase is the subject. The clause is restrictive throughout.
entries.variants: the extent to which (the commoner near-twin); the degree of + noun (the nominal version); how far, how much, how well (the plain substitutes)
entries.see also: the extent to which, in which, the manner in which, which

entries.meaning: The workhorse of the which frames, and the phrase American academic prose reaches for when it wants to ask how much without committing to an answer. It is a genuine hedge rather than mere padding: the extent to which the ruling still controls concedes in advance that the answer is partial, where whether the ruling still controls forces a yes or no. That is why editors who cut it to how far sometimes change the claim.
examples: The extent to which the contamination had spread was not known for weeks.
The study measures the extent to which households actually changed their driving.
The extent to which the two versions differ comes down to a single clause.
The auditors asked about the extent to which the estimates relied on management's own projections.
It is hard to overstate the extent to which that one decision shaped the department.
The brief argues about the extent to which the earlier ruling still controls.
entries.русский: то, насколько; мера, в какой — книжн.: стандартная осторожная формула
entries.register: formal; the standard hedge of academic, scientific, and official American prose
entries.type: complex relative frame — noun of measure + pied-piped preposition + relative pronoun
entries.clause type: restrictive relative clause modifying extent; the whole phrase behaves as a noun phrase
entries.pattern: The extent to which [subject] [verb] + [main verb] — the phrase as subject. · [verb of measuring/assessing] the extent to which [clause] — as object. · [preposition] the extent to which [clause]. · to the extent that [clause] — the related conditional frame, which is a different construction and lives with the comparison words.
entries.punctuation: No comma inside the frame and none between it and the main verb when the phrase is the subject — The extent to which the two versions differ is a matter of one clause takes nothing before is. Never a comma before to which.
entries.variants: the degree to which (the near-twin); how far, how much (the plain substitutes); the extent of + noun (the nominal version)
entries.see also: the degree to which, in which, the conditions under which, which

entries.meaning: The bulkiest of the which frames: the manner in which he answered is four words doing the work of how he answered. It survives for two honest reasons — it is genuinely more formal, and it lets a complaint, an opinion, or a personnel file describe conduct at arm's length without seeming to characterize it. Everywhere else it is padding, and how is the fix.
examples: The complaint objects to the manner in which the search was conducted.
The manner in which the layoffs were announced did more damage than the layoffs.
The statute prescribes the manner in which notice must be given to a tenant.
She testified at length about the manner in which the samples had been handled.
The manner in which he answered that one question told the panel everything.
The bylaws are silent as to the manner in which a tie vote is to be broken.
entries.русский: то, как; способ, которым — книжн., юр.; стилисты советуют заменять на how
entries.register: formal; legal, official, and old-fashioned expository prose — and the standing example, in every American style guide, of a phrase that ought to be how
entries.type: complex relative frame — noun of manner + pied-piped preposition + relative pronoun
entries.clause type: restrictive relative clause modifying manner; the whole phrase behaves as a noun phrase
entries.pattern: The manner in which [subject] [verb] + [main verb] — the phrase as subject. · [verb of describing/objecting to] the manner in which [clause] — as object. · [preposition] the manner in which [clause] — as in as to the manner in which. · in the manner in which [clause] — the doubled form, best avoided. · the manner whereby / the manner wherein — archaic.
entries.punctuation: No comma inside the frame; none between the frame and the main verb when the phrase is the subject. The clause is restrictive, so it never opens with a comma.
entries.variants: the way in which (a shade lighter, same construction); the way (that) (informal); how (the one-word equivalent, available in nearly every sentence either of the others appears in); the manner whereby, the manner wherein (archaic)
entries.see also: in which, the conditions under which, wherein, which, the way

entries.meaning: English once had a definite relative the which running alongside bare which, on the model of French lequel and Latin qui. It was ordinary for Chaucer, still available to Shakespeare, and gone from living prose by the eighteenth century. Nothing separates it from plain which in meaning — the article marked a definiteness that English relatives no longer mark at all — so a modern writer who reaches for it is quoting a period rather than drawing a distinction.
examples: He showed me the deed, the which I read twice before signing anything.
There followed a great silence, the which no man cared to break.
The king sent letters, in the which he named his successor.
She took a fever, the which held her a fortnight and more.
They came at last to a river, the which they could by no means cross.
He spoke much of his debts, of the which he had a great many.
entries.русский: каковой, который — устар. (Чосер, Шекспир): по смыслу ничем не отличается от which
entries.register: archaic; Middle and Early Modern English, and after about 1700 a deliberate costume — an American meets it in Chaucer, Malory, the 1611 Bible, and Shakespeare
entries.type: relative pronoun carrying a definite article
entries.clause type: relative clause, restrictive or nonrestrictive; also sentential, with a whole clause as antecedent
entries.pattern: [noun], the which [verb phrase] — nonrestrictive. · [noun] the which [subject] [verb] — restrictive. · [preposition] the which [clause] — as in of the which, in the which. · [clause], the which [clause] — sentential, the whole preceding clause as antecedent.
entries.punctuation: Pointed exactly like plain which: commas around a clause that merely adds, none around one that narrows. Be warned that Early Modern printing does not follow that rule reliably, so a period text will not confirm it — apply the modern rule when you write the form yourself.
entries.variants: plain which (the form that won and the only living one); the whiche (the Middle English spelling); of the which, in the which (the pied-piped versions)
entries.see also: which, that, he that, in which, whereof

entries.meaning: What is the relative with no antecedent: it swallows its own head, so what he said means "the thing that he said" in a single word. Contrast which and that, which both require a noun standing in front of them. Nonstandard American dialects use what as an ordinary relative (the man what fixed the roof), which is strongly marked.
examples: What he said in the meeting is not what he told me afterward.
I'll have what she's having.
What worries me is the timeline, not the budget.
She gave the movers what was left in the garage.
Tell me what the doctor actually said, not what you wish he'd said.
What the storm didn't take, the insurance company argued about for a year.
entries.русский: то, что — слитное относительное: само содержит свой антецедент («the thing which»)
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: fused relative pronoun; also an interrogative and an exclamative determiner
entries.clause type: nominal relative (free relative) clause — a clause that functions as a noun phrase
entries.pattern: What [clause] + [main verb] — the clause as subject. · [verb/preposition] what [clause] — the clause as object. · What [clause] is [complement] — the pseudo-cleft. · what + noun (what money we had left).
entries.punctuation: No comma between a what clause and the verb that goes with it — the clause is the subject or the object, and neither is ever cut off from its verb by a single comma. A fronted pseudo-cleft (What I need is a nap) likewise takes no comma.
entries.variants: whatever (the emphatic free relative); that which (the stiff formal equivalent)

entries.meaning: The all is not the ordinary quantifier floating loose but an exhaustiveness marker fixed to the wh- word: What did he say? invites one answer, What all did he say? asks for the complete list. Standard English has to paraphrase that distinction with everything that, which is exactly why the construction stays so stable in the regions that have it. Note that it can also head a free relative (what all he did with the money), where standard English would need everything he did.
examples: What all did the mechanic say was wrong with it?
I don't know what all she put in that casserole.
Tell me what all I need to bring on Saturday.
What all he did with the money never came out at trial.
He'll tell you what all is wrong with this county in about four minutes.
Nobody had written down what all was promised at that meeting.
entries.pronunciation note: casually /ˈwʌɾ ˌɔl/, with the t flapped · WUT-awl
entries.русский: что именно; всё то, что — диал. (юг США): вопрос требует полного перечня
entries.register: dialectal — Southern and South Midland American, and heard well beyond that in casual speech; absent from edited prose
entries.type: fused relative and interrogative pronoun carrying exhaustive all
entries.clause type: noun clause (indirect question, exhaustive); nominal relative clause
entries.pattern: What all [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? — direct question. · [verb of asking/knowing/telling] what all [subject] [verb] — embedded, statement word order. · What all [verb phrase] + [main verb] — the clause as subject. · what all + noun + [clause] — as in what all paperwork they need. · What [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] all? — the all floated to the end.
entries.punctuation: No comma between what and all, and none before the embedded clause. A direct question takes a question mark; the embedded clause takes none.
entries.variants: who all, where all, how all (the same all on the other wh- words); everything that, all the things (that) (the standard paraphrases)
entries.see also: what, who all, where all, whatever

entries.meaning: Refers to things, animals, and ideas — never to people, who take who. The American that/which convention: use that for a clause that narrows which thing you mean, and which with commas for a clause that adds a detail about a thing already identified. Which has one power that lacks: it can take an entire preceding clause as its antecedent (He was late, which surprised no one).
examples: Her first novel, which took eleven years to write, sold four thousand copies.
The bridge, which was rebuilt in 2004, is closed for repairs again.
He missed the filing deadline, which surprised absolutely no one.
This is the cabinet in which the old contracts were stored.
