They moved in June, by which time the roof was already leaking.
The recipe calls for pancetta, which you can replace with bacon.
entries.русский: который; что — о предметах; в амер. норме неограничительное, с запятыми
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: relative pronoun; also an interrogative determiner
entries.clause type: relative clause — nonrestrictive in edited American prose, restrictive after a preposition
entries.pattern: [noun], which [clause], [rest of sentence]. · [noun] [preposition] which [clause]. · [independent clause], which [clause] — sentential relative. · which + noun (by which time, at which point).
entries.punctuation: A nonrestrictive which clause is fenced by commas on both sides — one before it, and one after it if the sentence continues. Dropping that closing comma is the most common punctuation error with this word: Her novel, which took eleven years to write sold four thousand copies is wrong. When which follows a preposition (the box in which it came), the clause is restrictive and takes no commas.
entries.variants: that (restrictive equivalent, no commas); of which (possessive alternative to whose)

entries.meaning: The people relative. In everyday American English who has annexed most of whom's territory, so the guy who I met is normal speech and the guy whom I met is formal writing. The one place whom is still required is directly after a preposition.
examples: The woman who called about the sofa never showed up.
My neighbor, who teaches at the middle school, waters our plants in August.
Anyone who wants seconds should speak up now.
I have no idea who left the back door open.
She's the one who actually fixed the sprinkler system.
Kids who eat breakfast test better — that's the entire finding.
entries.русский: кто; который — о людях, форма подлежащего
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: relative pronoun (subject case); also an interrogative
entries.clause type: relative clause, restrictive or nonrestrictive; noun clause (indirect question)
entries.pattern: [person noun] who [verb phrase] — subject relative, restrictive. · [person noun], who [verb phrase], [rest of sentence] — subject relative, nonrestrictive. · [person noun] who [subject] [verb] — object relative, normal in speech where formal writing takes whom. · [verb of knowing/asking] who [clause] — indirect question.
entries.punctuation: No commas when the clause identifies which person is meant (the woman who called). Commas on both sides when the person is already identified (my sister, who called Tuesday, is coming). Because a proper name is already fully identified, a relative clause after a name is nearly always nonrestrictive and therefore takes commas.
entries.variants: that (acceptable restrictive alternative for people, slightly less formal); whom (object case); whose (possessive)

entries.meaning: Asks for a full roster rather than a single name: Who came? can be answered with one person, Who all came? asks for everybody. The construction has a grammar of its own — the all can float away from who (Who did you invite all?), and it takes a possessive (who all's truck is in the driveway?) — which is why it is best analyzed as a plural interrogative pronoun rather than as a loose quantifier that happens to be standing nearby.
examples: Who all is coming to the reunion this year?
I never found out who all signed that letter.
Who all's truck is parked behind the shed?
She wanted to know who all he'd talked to before he called her.
Who all did they end up laying off?
There is no record of who all was in the room that afternoon.
entries.русский: кто именно; все, кто — диал. (юг США): вопрос требует перечислить всех
entries.register: dialectal — Southern and South Midland American; ordinary in speech across that region and absent from edited prose
entries.type: interrogative and relative pronoun carrying exhaustive all
entries.clause type: noun clause (indirect question, exhaustive); relative clause
entries.pattern: Who all [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? — direct question. · Who all [verb phrase]? — as subject of its own question. · [verb of asking/knowing] who all [verb phrase] — embedded, statement word order. · who all's + noun — the possessive, as in who all's car is that. · Who [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] all? — the all floated to the end.
entries.punctuation: No comma between who and all, and none before the embedded clause. Direct questions take a question mark. Note the contracted possessive: it is written who all's, with the apostrophe on all, never whose all.
entries.variants: what all, where all (the same construction on other wh- words); y'all (the same all fused onto you); everyone who, which of them (the standard paraphrases)
entries.see also: who, what all, where all, whoever, whom

entries.meaning: The object form of who. The reliable test: rebuild the relative clause as a plain sentence and try he versus him — if him fits, whom is correct (the committee selected him → the candidate whom the committee selected). In practice whom is obligatory only right after a preposition; elsewhere American speech uses who, and overcorrecting to whom in subject position (the man whom called) is worse than using who.
examples: To whom it may concern.
The candidate whom the committee selected withdrew a week later.
My grandmother, whom I saw maybe twice a year, sent a card every single week.
The people with whom he shared the house never learned his last name.
I have no idea whom they'll appoint to the vacancy.
She's the attorney for whom I clerked right out of law school.
entries.русский: кого, кому — объектная форма who; книжн., обязательна после предлога
entries.register: formal
entries.type: relative pronoun (object case); also an interrogative
entries.clause type: relative clause, restrictive or nonrestrictive; noun clause (indirect question)
entries.pattern: [noun] whom [subject] [verb] — object relative. · [noun] [preposition] whom [clause] — pied-piped, as in the people with whom he lived. · [noun], whom [clause], [rest of sentence] — nonrestrictive.
entries.punctuation: The same restrictive/nonrestrictive comma rule as who. Never a comma between a preposition and whom.
entries.variants: who (the normal informal substitute in every position except immediately after a preposition); whomever

entries.meaning: The possessive relative, and the only relative word that is a determiner rather than a pronoun — it must be followed by a noun. It is not restricted to people, despite a stubborn myth: a house whose roof leaks is standard American English, and the alternative a house the roof of which leaks is stiff enough that even careful editors avoid it.
examples: The family whose dog got out lives two doors down.
My cousin, whose flight was canceled, ended up driving nine hours overnight.
It's an old building whose wiring nobody wants to touch.
Students whose names appear on this list should report to the front office.
No one could figure out whose car was blocking the alley.
A company whose only real asset is one patent is a risky bet.
entries.русский: чей; которого — притяжательное относительное, о людях и (реже) о предметах
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: relative determiner (possessive); also an interrogative
entries.clause type: relative clause, restrictive or nonrestrictive; noun clause (indirect question)
entries.pattern: [noun] whose [noun] [verb] — the possessed noun always follows immediately. · [noun], whose [noun] [clause], [rest of sentence]. · [preposition] whose [noun] [clause]. · [verb of knowing/asking] whose [noun] [clause].
entries.punctuation: The standard restrictive/nonrestrictive comma rule. Never a comma between whose and the noun it possesses — they form one phrase.
entries.variants: of which (the stiff alternative for inanimate antecedents); whosever (rare); note that who's is a contraction of who is and is never the possessive

entries.ipa: ∅ — unpronounced; the clause simply begins with its own subject
entries.meaning: The commonest relative in American speech is no word at all. Deletion is licensed in exactly one environment: a restrictive clause in which the relative word would have been the object of the verb or of a preposition. It is blocked when the relative word would be the subject (the email that arrived — you cannot say the email arrived and mean the same thing), blocked in every nonrestrictive clause, and blocked after a pied-piped preposition (the people with whom he lived, never the people with he lived). The three relative adverbs delete on the same terms, which is why the day we met and the town I grew up in need no connector either. ---
examples: The email ∅ I sent Tuesday never got a reply.
That's the chair ∅ she always sits in.
The guy ∅ we hired in March already quit.
It's the one thing ∅ nobody wants to talk about.
Remember the summer ∅ the power went out for nine days?
The reason ∅ I called is that the check never cleared.
That's not the town ∅ I grew up in.
entries.русский: нулевое относительное — пропуск which/that/whom-дополнения; в русском так опустить нельзя
entries.register: neutral; the ordinary spoken choice
entries.type: relative pronoun (null)
entries.clause type: restrictive relative clause only, and only when the missing word is the object
entries.pattern: [noun] ∅ [subject] [verb] — object relative, as in the email I sent. · [noun] ∅ [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded preposition, as in the chair she sat on. · [time noun] ∅ [clause] — the day we met. · [place noun] ∅ [clause] — the town I grew up in. · the reason ∅ [clause] — the reason I left.
entries.punctuation: No comma, ever. A comma would mark the clause as nonrestrictive, and a nonrestrictive clause cannot drop its relative word — my brother, I met at the airport, was late is not English. The gap is also the reason no comma may separate the antecedent from the clause: the email, I sent yesterday is an error, not a pause.
entries.variants: the overt that, which, who, whom, when, where, why — any of which can be restored
entries.see also: that, which, whom, when, where, why, zero that

entries.meaning: This entry covers when as a relative adverb — the word that hooks a clause onto a time noun. Its far more common life as an adverbial conjunction (Call me when you land) belongs with the time subordinators, and the test between them is simple: a relative when has a time noun sitting in front of it that the clause modifies; an adverbial when modifies the verb and has no antecedent at all.
examples: That was the summer when everything changed.
There are days when nothing in this building works.
August, when half the staff is on vacation, is the worst possible month to launch.
I remember the exact moment when the power came back on.
Nobody told us when the inspection was scheduled.
He's holding out for a time when interest rates finally come down.
entries.русский: когда; в который — относительное наречие при существительном времени
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: relative adverb; also a subordinating conjunction of time and an interrogative
entries.clause type: relative clause modifying a time noun; noun clause (indirect question)
entries.pattern: [time noun] when [clause] — restrictive. · [time noun], when [clause], [rest of sentence] — nonrestrictive. · [time noun] ∅ [clause] — relative when deleted. · [verb of knowing/asking] when [clause].
entries.punctuation: No commas when the clause specifies which time is meant (the day when we met). Commas on both sides when the time is already fixed (last Tuesday, when we met, was miserable). Never a comma before an indirect question.
entries.variants: that, or nothing at all (the day we met); on which / in which / at which (formal equivalents)

entries.meaning: The most restricted of the three relative adverbs: its antecedent is essentially always the noun reason. The reason why is often attacked as redundant; it is not ungrammatical, and it has been in continuous use for centuries, but the reason I left and why I left are both leaner and neither loses anything. ---
examples: The reason why the bridge failed is still under investigation.
Nobody can explain why the printer only jams on Mondays.
That is exactly why I keep a spare key in the garage.
Why the company waited three weeks to disclose it is the real question.
There's no reason why we can't start an hour early.
She never told anyone why she quit.
entries.русский: почему; по которой — относительное наречие только при слове reason
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: relative adverb; also an interrogative
entries.clause type: relative clause modifying reason; noun clause (indirect question)
entries.pattern: the reason [why] [clause] — the why is optional. · [verb of knowing/asking] why [clause]. · Why [clause] + [main verb] — the clause as subject, as in Why he left is still a mystery. · That's why [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before relative why, and none before an indirect question. When a why clause is the subject of the sentence, no comma separates it from its verb.
entries.variants: the zero relative (the reason I left); that (the reason that I left); for which (formal)

entries.meaning: Not a separate word but a metrical spelling: -ever collapses to -e'er so the line scans one syllable shorter. Each member of the set contracts a different base word — whate'er is whatever, where'er is wherever, whoe'er is whoever, whene'er is whenever, howe'er is however — and every one of them keeps the grammar, the clause type, and the commas of the word it stands for. They are collected under one heading here because the elision, not the individual word, is the thing to recognize: it announces verse, hymnody, or deliberate pastiche, and never anything else.
examples: Whate'er betide, I shall not leave thee.
Whene'er he passed the churchyard gate, he lowered his eyes.
Where'er the pilgrim turned, the road ran uphill.
Howe'er the world may judge, my conscience holds.
Whoe'er thou art that readest this, pray for the mason.
Take whate'er thou wilt, and leave me but the ring.
entries.pronunciation note: wut-AIR — two syllables where whatever has three, which is the entire reason the spelling exists
entries.русский: что бы ни — устар., поэт.: стяжённое whatever
entries.register: archaic and poetic — hymn text, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century verse, and Shakespeare; in modern prose it is period costume and nothing else
entries.type: fused relative pronoun and determiner; also a concessive subordinator
entries.clause type: nominal relative clause; concessive adverbial clause
entries.pattern: Whate'er [clause] + [main verb] — clause as subject. · [verb/preposition] whate'er [clause] — clause as object. · Whate'er [clause], [main clause] — concessive. · the same elision on the rest of the family: whene'er (= whenever), where'er (= wherever), howe'er (= however), whoe'er (= whoever).
entries.punctuation: Identical to the uncontracted forms — no comma when the clause fills a noun slot, comma after a fronted concessive clause. The apostrophe replaces the v of -ever and nothing else: there is no second apostrophe, no space, and no hyphen.
entries.variants: whene'er, where'er, howe'er, whoe'er, whatso'er, whereso'er (the rest of the elided family); ne'er, e'er, o'er (the same elision on ordinary words); the full forms whatever, wherever, whoever, whenever, however

entries.meaning: Means "anything that" in the nominal use and "no matter what" in the concessive one. Against plain what: what is neutral and specific ("the thing that"), while whatever is free-choice and waves away the alternatives. Against whichever: whatever draws from an open field, whichever from a known set.
examples: Whatever you decide, I'll back you all the way.
Whatever is left in the fridge on Sunday is fair game.
Take whatever you need from the supply closet.
Whatever time you get in tonight, text me.
He'll argue about whatever you put in front of him.
Whatever the survey said, the customers are obviously unhappy.
entries.pronunciation note: casually /wəˈɾɛvər/, with the t flapped · wut-EV-er
entries.русский: что бы ни; всё, что — слитное относительное и уступительное
entries.register: neutral; the standalone dismissive Whatever. is very informal
entries.type: fused relative pronoun and determiner; also a concessive subordinator
entries.clause type: nominal relative clause (acting as a noun phrase); concessive adverbial clause
entries.pattern: Whatever [clause] + [main verb] — clause as subject. · [verb/preposition] whatever [clause] — clause as object. · Whatever [clause], [main clause] — concessive. · whatever + noun + [clause] (whatever time you get in).
entries.punctuation: No comma when the whatever clause is the subject or object of the main verb (Whatever you decide is fine with me). Comma when it is a fronted concessive adverbial (Whatever you decide, I'll back you). Same word, two structures, and the comma is what tells them apart.
entries.variants: whatsoever (emphatic, formal); what ever as two words only in an emphatic question (What ever were you thinking?)

entries.meaning: Historically the emphatic form of whatever, built with the intensifying suffix -soever. In modern American English it has almost stopped being a relative pronoun: nearly all of its uses are the tag after a negated noun, where it means "at all." It must follow the noun — no whatsoever reason is not English — and it needs a negative to attach to, which is why there is evidence whatsoever sounds broken.
examples: There is no evidence whatsoever that the supplement does anything.
She had no interest whatsoever in going back to that job.
"Any objection?" "None whatsoever."
The lease gives the tenant no right whatsoever to sublet the unit.
He offered no explanation whatsoever for the missing three hours.
"Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might."
entries.русский: какой бы то ни было; совершенно никакой — усилитель после отрицаемого существительного
entries.register: formal; the negative-tag use is neutral
entries.type: emphatic fused relative; in modern use chiefly a negative-polarity intensifier
entries.clause type: nominal relative clause (archaic); in modern use, no clause at all — a postmodifier attached to a negated noun
entries.pattern: no [noun] whatsoever. · none whatsoever. · not … any [noun] whatsoever. · Whatsoever [clause], [main clause] — archaic.
entries.punctuation: No comma before it in the negative-intensifier use — it sits immediately after the noun it strengthens and belongs to the same phrase. The archaic clausal use follows the wheresoever rule: comma after a fronted clause.
entries.variants: whatever (equally correct in the negative-tag slot: no reason whatever); whatso (archaic)

entries.meaning: The selective free relative. Whatever leaves the field wide open; whichever picks from a known, closed set — two flavors on the counter get whichever, an unlimited menu gets whatever. Its fixed tag whichever comes first is standard in warranties, leases, and statutes.
examples: Take whichever seat is open.
Whichever route you pick, you'll hit construction somewhere.
The warranty runs three years or 36,000 miles, whichever comes first.
He'll happily eat whichever one you don't want.
Whichever of the two bids comes in lower will get the contract.
Call the office or email us, whichever is easier for you.
entries.русский: какой бы ни; тот из них, который — выбор из известного набора
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: fused relative pronoun and determiner; also a concessive subordinator (Whichever way you go, allow an hour)
entries.clause type: nominal relative clause; concessive adverbial clause
entries.pattern: [verb] whichever [clause] — clause as object. · Whichever [clause] + [main verb] — clause as subject. · whichever + noun + [clause] (whichever route you pick). · Whichever [clause], [main clause] — concessive. · …, whichever [comes first / is greater] — fixed contractual tag.
entries.punctuation: No comma when the clause is the subject or object of the main verb. Comma after a fronted concessive whichever clause. The contractual tag always takes a comma before it: three years or 36,000 miles, whichever comes first.
entries.variants: whichsoever (archaic, legal)

entries.meaning: The -soever partner of whichever, and functionally identical to it: the suffix adds period weight, not meaning or emphasis. One habitat is left to it — the closed-set tag in older insurance policies, leases, and wills (whichsoever shall first occur), which drafters preserve because that exact wording has been litigated for two centuries while whichever has not been litigated in that particular document. Outside drafting it reads as costume, exactly like whosoever.
examples: The term ends in ten years or upon the death of the survivor, whichsoever shall first occur.
The insurer shall pay the cost of repair or the actual cash value, whichsoever is the lesser.
Whichsoever of the two remedies the buyer elects, the seller's liability is capped at the purchase price.
The executor may sell or retain the shares, whichsoever course he judges best for the estate.
Notice may be given by mail or by hand, whichsoever method the parties have last agreed upon.
Whichsoever road the commissioners choose, the mill will object to it.
entries.русский: какой бы ни — устар., юр.: усиленное whichever, в старых полисах и завещаниях
entries.register: archaic; survives only in older policies, leases, and wills, and even there whichever has all but replaced it
entries.type: emphatic fused relative pronoun and determiner; also a concessive subordinator
entries.clause type: nominal relative clause; concessive adverbial clause
entries.pattern: [verb] whichsoever [clause] — clause as object. · whichsoever + noun + [clause] — as in whichsoever remedy the buyer elects. · Whichsoever [clause], [main clause] — concessive. · …, whichsoever [shall first occur / is the lesser] — the contractual tag.
entries.punctuation: The whichever rules exactly: no comma when the clause fills a noun slot, comma after a fronted concessive clause, and always a comma before the contractual tag — ten years or the death of the survivor, whichsoever shall first occur.
entries.variants: whichever (the living equivalent in every sense); whatsoever, whosoever, whomsoever, wheresoever (the rest of the -soever family)

entries.meaning: Means "anyone who," "the person who," or, concessively, "no matter who." The case trap is the thing to learn: whoever takes its case from its job inside its own clause, not from the outer sentence. Give it to whoever answers the door is correct — whoever is the subject of answers, and the whole clause, not the single word, is the object of to.
examples: Whoever parked in my spot is getting towed.
Give the extra ticket to whoever shows up first.
Whoever wrote this manual has clearly never used the machine.
Whoever you talk to over there, get it in writing.
She'll beat whoever runs against her in November.
Whoever left the milk out on the counter, please deal with it.
entries.русский: кто бы ни; тот, кто — слитное относительное, форма подлежащего
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: fused relative pronoun (subject case); also a concessive subordinator (Whoever calls, I'm out)
entries.clause type: nominal relative clause; concessive adverbial clause
entries.pattern: Whoever [verb phrase] + [main verb] — clause as subject. · [verb/preposition] whoever [verb phrase] — clause as object of the outer verb, but whoever is still the subject inside. · Whoever [clause], [main clause] — concessive.
entries.punctuation: No comma between a subject whoever clause and the main verb, and none between a preposition and whoever. Comma after a fronted concessive whoever clause (Whoever you talk to, get it in writing).
entries.variants: whosoever (archaic, biblical); whoso (archaic); whomever (object case inside the clause); whosever (rare possessive)

entries.meaning: Correct only when the word is the object inside its own clause: She'll hire whomever the committee recommends (object of recommends) versus She'll hire whoever applies (subject of applies). Because writers reach for whomever by reflex whenever a preposition precedes it, the commonest error in American prose is send it to whomever answers the phone, which should be whoever — the preposition governs the whole clause, not the pronoun.
examples: Send the invoice to whomever the client designates.
She'll hire whomever the committee recommends.
He was willing to sell the truck to whomever he could find.
Address the letter to whomever you spoke with last week.
The award goes to whomever the judges pick, and there's no appeal.
Bring whomever you like to the reception — there's plenty of food.
The senior partner will assign the case to whomever she trusts most.
entries.русский: кого бы ни; того, кого — книжн.: объектная форма whoever
entries.register: formal
entries.type: fused relative pronoun (object case)
entries.clause type: nominal relative clause
entries.pattern: [verb] whomever [subject] [verb] — object inside its own clause. · [main clause] [preposition] whomever [subject] [verb] — as in to whomever the client designates, where the preposition governs the whole clause, not the pronoun. · [verb] whomever [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded, as in whomever you spoke with.
entries.punctuation: No comma before it, and none between a preposition and whomever.
entries.variants: whoever (the ordinary spoken substitute); whomsoever (archaic, legal)

entries.meaning: The -soever partner of whomever, and correct on exactly the same terms: only when the word is the object inside its own clause. The estate passes to whomsoever the executor names is right, because whomsoever is the object of names; the estate passes to whomsoever survives him is a hypercorrection, because there the word is the subject of survives and whosoever is wanted. Outside estate drafting and deliberate period pastiche it reads as costume, not formality.
examples: The residue shall be distributed to whomsoever the trustee may designate in writing.
She addressed the letter, half seriously, to whomsoever it might concern.
Whomsoever the committee names, the appointment takes effect in January.
The king granted the charter to whomsoever his council recommended.
He promised the parcel to whomsoever he found first.
The bounty is payable to whomsoever the sheriff shall approve.
entries.русский: кого бы ни — устар., юр.: объектная форма whosoever, в завещаниях и трастах
entries.register: archaic; survives in wills, trusts, and set formulas — never neutral
entries.type: fused relative pronoun (object case)
entries.clause type: nominal relative clause
entries.pattern: [verb] whomsoever [subject] [verb] — object inside its own clause. · [preposition] whomsoever [subject] [verb] — as in to whomsoever the trustee shall designate. · Whomsoever [subject] [verb], [main clause] — fronted concessive. · to whomsoever it may concern — the fixed salutation.
entries.punctuation: No comma before it, and none between a preposition and whomsoever. A comma appears only when the clause is fronted as a concessive (Whomsoever the committee names, the term begins in January).
entries.variants: whomever (the living equivalent); whoever (the ordinary spoken substitute); whosoever (subject case)

entries.meaning: The -soever member of the whoever family, built with the same intensifying suffix as wheresoever and whatsoever, and meaning "any person at all who." It is not a stylistic upgrade on whoever — it is a period costume, and outside scripture, hymnody, and statutory drafting it reads as parody. Its object form whomsoever follows the same rule as whomever: it is correct only when the pronoun is the object inside its own clause, so to whomsoever shall apply is a hypercorrection for to whosoever shall apply. --- ← The grammar of conjunctions · All categories
examples: "Whosoever shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father."
The trust shall pay the balance to whosoever survives the settlor.
Whosoever drafted this indemnity clause did not read the rest of the contract.
Whosoever the next tenant turns out to be, the easement runs with the land.
The reward is offered to whosoever returns the manuscript intact.
She addressed the letter, half seriously, to whomsoever it might concern.
entries.русский: кто бы ни; всякий, кто — устар., библ.: усиленное whoever
entries.register: archaic; survives in scripture, hymn text, and legal drafting — never neutral
entries.type: fused relative pronoun (subject case); also a concessive subordinator
entries.clause type: nominal relative clause; concessive adverbial clause
entries.pattern: Whosoever [verb phrase] + [main verb] — clause as subject. · [verb/preposition] whosoever [verb phrase] — clause as object of the outer verb, with whosoever still the subject inside. · Whosoever [clause], [main clause] — concessive. · to whomsoever [clause] — the object partner, used after a preposition that governs the pronoun itself.
entries.punctuation: No comma between a subject whosoever clause and the main verb, and none between a preposition and whosoever. Comma after a fronted concessive clause, exactly as with whoever. The King James comma after the subject clause (Whosoever believeth in him, should not perish) is seventeenth-century practice and is an error today.
entries.variants: whoever (the living equivalent in every sense); whomsoever (object case); whoso (older still); whosesoever (rare possessive)
